questions.question: Describe the importance of propagules in floriculture.
questions.solution_html:
• Ans: Propagules are plant parts used to produce new plants, such as seeds, cuttings
  • bulbs, suckers, runners, and tubers. Their importance includes
  • Mass multiplication: Helps in producing large numbers of ornamental plants quickly.
  • True-to-type plants: Vegetative propagules ensure offspring are genetically identical
  • to the parent plant (important for maintaining flower color and shape).
  • Faster flowering: Propagules like bulbs, rhizomes, and cuttings reach maturity faster
  • compared to seeds.
  • Seasonal availability: Some ornamental plants do not produce viable seeds; hence
  • propagules are the only means of propagation (e.g., chrysanthemum, rose).
  • Cost-effective for nurseries: Reduces production time and cost, which benefits
  • commercial floriculture.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Describe the factors influencing seed dormancy.
questions.solution_html:
• Ans: Seed dormancy is a condition where seeds do not germinate even under
  • favorable conditions. Factors include
  • Hard seed coat: Prevents water and oxygen entry (e.g., legumes).
  • Immature embryo: Embryo is not fully developed at the time of seed dispersal.
  • Chemical inhibitors: Presence of growth-inhibiting substances like abscisic acid or
  • phenolic compounds in seed coat.
  • Temperature and light: Some seeds need specific temperatures or light conditions to
  • break dormancy (e.g., lettuce).
  • Environmental conditions: Dryness or lack of moisture can keep seeds dormant.
questions.final_answer: Environmental conditions: Dryness or lack of moisture can keep seeds dormant
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Describe the effect of hormonal treatment (Natural & Artificial) on plant / propagation.
questions.solution_html:
• Ans: Plant hormones (phytohormones) play a major role in plant propagation.
  • Auxins (e.g., IAA, IBA, NAA): Promote root formation in stem and leaf cuttings.
  • Used in rooting powders.
  • Cytokinins (e.g., kinetin, BAP): Encourage shoot formation and delay leaf aging.
  • Used in tissue culture.
  • Gibberellins: Break seed dormancy and promote seed germination and stem
  • elongation.
  • Ethylene: Helps in fruit ripening and flower opening.
  • Artificial hormones: Synthetic forms like IBA and NAA are widely used in nurseries
  • to improve rooting success and survival rate in plant propagation
questions.final_answer: to improve rooting success and survival rate in plant propagation

questions.question: Describe the cultivation practices and post-harvesting uses of Jackfruit.
questions.solution_html:
• Ans
  • Cultivation Practices
  • Climate and Soil
  • Jackfruit grows well in warm, humid tropical climates with annual rainfall of
  • 150–200 cm. It prefers deep, well-drained loamy soil rich in organic matter and
  • slightly acidic pH (6.0–6.5).
  • Propagation
  • It is propagated by seeds, but for true-to-type plants, vegetative methods such as
  • inarching, budding, or grafting are preferred.
  • Planting
  • Pits of about 1 m³ are dug and filled with a mixture of topsoil and organic manure.
  • Recommended spacing is 8–10 m apart. Planting is usually done at the onset of
  • monsoon.
  • Manuring and Fertilization
  • Application of FYM (20–25 kg/tree/year) along with NPK fertilizers promotes
  • healthy growth and early fruiting.
  • Irrigation
  • Regular watering is essential during the dry season, especially for young plants.
  • Mature trees tolerate short dry periods.
  • Pruning and Training
  • Removal of dead and overcrowded branches helps in better sunlight penetration and
  • fruit quality.
  • Pest and Disease Management
  • Common pests include shoot borers and fruit flies; bagging of fruits and use of
  • neem-based sprays help reduce damage.
  • Harvesting
  • Fruits are harvested 3–8 months after flowering when they emit a dull sound on
  • tapping and spines become well developed.
  • Post-Harvest Uses
  • Nutritional Use: The ripe bulbs are rich in carbohydrates, vitamins A and C, and are
  • eaten fresh or used in jams, jellies, and desserts.
  • Vegetable Use: The immature green fruit is cooked as a popular vegetable or used in
  • pickles and curries.
  • Processed Products: Chips, dehydrated flakes, and jackfruit flour are now
  • commercially produced.
  • Seed Utilization: Seeds are edible when roasted or boiled and are a good source of
  • starch and protein.
  • Wood Use: The timber is durable, termite-resistant, and used in furniture and musical
  • instruments.

questions.question: Describe fertigation.
questions.solution_html:
• Ans: Fertigation is a highly efficient agricultural technique that combines fertilization
  • and irrigation by injecting soluble fertilizers directly into the water stream of a
  • pressurized irrigation system, most commonly drip irrigation. This method ensures
  • that water and precise doses of nutrients are delivered simultaneously and directly to
  • the active root zone of the crops. The primary advantages of fertigation include a
  • significant increase in nutrient-use efficiency, substantial water savings, and the
  • ability to apply nutrients exactly when the plant needs them for optimal growth
  • resulting in higher yields and reduced environmental impact compared to traditional
  • broadcast methods.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Write a short essay on effect of soil factors on irrigation.
questions.solution_html:
• Ans: Soil acts as the water reservoir for the plants. Its properties govern how often
  • and how much water must be applied.
  • ● Soil Texture (Sand, Silt, Clay)
  • ○ Sandy Soils: Have large pores, a high infiltration rate (water soaks in quickly)
  • and a low water-holding capacity (it drains out quickly). They require
  • frequent, small irrigation applications.
  • ○ Clay Soils: Have very fine pores, a low infiltration rate (water soaks in
  • slowly), and a high water-holding capacity (it stores water for longer). They
  • can handle less frequent, larger applications, but application rates must be
  • slow to prevent runoff.
  • ● Soil Depth: Deeper soils can store more water, meaning they can sustain a crop for
  • longer periods between irrigations compared to shallow soils.
  • ● Topography (Slope): Fields with steep or uneven slopes are prone to runoff and
  • erosion under surface irrigation (like flood). Pressurized systems (sprinkler or drip)
  • are often preferred as they allow for more controlled application on sloped terrain.
  • Essay Questions

questions.question: Write an essay on advantages and disadvantages of Intercropping.
questions.solution_html:
• Ans: Intercropping is a method of growing more than one crop in the same piece of
  • land during the same crop season. This is an environmentally friendly pest control
  • crop protection, and yield enhancement approach.
  • Advantages of intercropping
  • • Better utilization of growth resources like nutrients, light, and moisture.
  • • Mitigate losses where the failure of any one of the component crops occurs.
  • • A farmer can get extra yield and, thereby, extra income from the unit area.
  • • Better utilization of space is available with the time dimensions.
  • • We can achieve better weed control by growing intercrops.
  • • Minimizes the chances of soil crust formation.
  • • Mitigate losses where the failure of any one of the component crops occurs.
  • • Intercrops will also enhance soil fertility.
  • • Controls soil erosion.
  • • To some extent, the pests and diseases of the main crop are controlled.
  • • Ecological stability.
  • • Cultivation practices for the major crop will also supplement companion crop
  • requirements.
  • • It provides shading and physical support to some crops.
  • • It provides daily needs for the farmers.
  • Disadvantages of intercropping
  • • Sometimes, intercrops work as alternate hosts for various pests and diseases.
  • • Differential maturity and sometimes harvesting may become a problem.
  • • It becomes difficult to control various pests and diseases.
  • • Intercropping is a labor-intensive practice.
  • • Allelopathic effect. (Plants produce biochemicals that influence the growth and
  • reproduction of others.)
  • • Possibility of problems in carrying out intercultural operations.
  • • Difficulty in mechanization for processes like crop cutting, spraying, and irrigation.
  • • There might be competition among the component crops.
questions.final_answer: • There might be competition among the component crops
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Describe the importance of propagules in floriculture.
questions.solution_html:
• Ans: Propagules are plant parts used to produce new plants, such as seeds, cuttings
  • bulbs, suckers, runners, and tubers. Their importance includes
  • Mass multiplication: Helps in producing large numbers of ornamental plants quickly.
  • True-to-type plants: Vegetative propagules ensure offspring are genetically identical
  • to the parent plant (important for maintaining flower color and shape).
  • Faster flowering: Propagules like bulbs, rhizomes, and cuttings reach maturity faster
  • compared to seeds.
  • Seasonal availability: Some ornamental plants do not produce viable seeds; hence
  • propagules are the only means of propagation (e.g., chrysanthemum, rose).
  • Cost-effective for nurseries: Reduces production time and cost, which benefits
  • commercial floriculture.

questions.question: Describe the factors influencing seed dormancy.
questions.solution_html:
• Ans: Seed dormancy is a condition where seeds do not germinate even under
  • favorable conditions. Factors include
  • Hard seed coat: Prevents water and oxygen entry (e.g., legumes).
  • Immature embryo: Embryo is not fully developed at the time of seed dispersal.
  • Chemical inhibitors: Presence of growth-inhibiting substances like abscisic acid or
  • phenolic compounds in seed coat.
  • Temperature and light: Some seeds need specific temperatures or light conditions to
  • break dormancy (e.g., lettuce).
  • Environmental conditions: Dryness or lack of moisture can keep seeds dormant.
questions.final_answer: Environmental conditions: Dryness or lack of moisture can keep seeds dormant

questions.question: Describe the cultivation practices and post-harvesting uses of Jackfruit.
questions.solution_html:
• Ans
  • Cultivation Practices
  • Climate and Soil
  • Jackfruit grows well in warm, humid tropical climates with annual rainfall of
  • 150–200 cm. It prefers deep, well-drained loamy soil rich in organic matter and
  • slightly acidic pH (6.0–6.5).
  • Propagation
  • It is propagated by seeds, but for true-to-type plants, vegetative methods such as
  • inarching, budding, or grafting are preferred.
  • Planting
  • Pits of about 1 m³ are dug and filled with a mixture of topsoil and organic manure.
  • Recommended spacing is 8–10 m apart. Planting is usually done at the onset of
  • monsoon.
  • Manuring and Fertilization
  • Application of FYM (20–25 kg/tree/year) along with NPK fertilizers promotes
  • healthy growth and early fruiting.
  • Irrigation
  • Regular watering is essential during the dry season, especially for young plants.
  • Mature trees tolerate short dry periods.
  • Pruning and Training
  • Removal of dead and overcrowded branches helps in better sunlight penetration and
  • fruit quality.
  • Pest and Disease Management
  • Common pests include shoot borers and fruit flies; bagging of fruits and use of
  • neem-based sprays help reduce damage.
  • Harvesting
  • Fruits are harvested 3–8 months after flowering when they emit a dull sound on
  • tapping and spines become well developed.
  • Post-Harvest Uses
  • Nutritional Use: The ripe bulbs are rich in carbohydrates, vitamins A and C, and are
  • eaten fresh or used in jams, jellies, and desserts.
  • Vegetable Use: The immature green fruit is cooked as a popular vegetable or used in
  • pickles and curries.
  • Processed Products: Chips, dehydrated flakes, and jackfruit flour are now
  • commercially produced.
  • Seed Utilization: Seeds are edible when roasted or boiled and are a good source of
  • starch and protein.
  • Wood Use: The timber is durable, termite-resistant, and used in furniture and musical
  • instruments.

questions.question: Describe fertigation.
questions.solution_html:
• Ans: Fertigation is a highly efficient agricultural technique that combines fertilization
  • and irrigation by injecting soluble fertilizers directly into the water stream of a
  • pressurized irrigation system, most commonly drip irrigation. This method ensures
  • that water and precise doses of nutrients are delivered simultaneously and directly to
  • the active root zone of the crops. The primary advantages of fertigation include a
  • significant increase in nutrient-use efficiency, substantial water savings, and the
  • ability to apply nutrients exactly when the plant needs them for optimal growth
  • resulting in higher yields and reduced environmental impact compared to traditional
  • broadcast methods.

questions.question: Write a short essay on effect of soil factors on irrigation.
questions.solution_html:
• Ans: Soil acts as the water reservoir for the plants. Its properties govern how often
  • and how much water must be applied.
  • ● Soil Texture (Sand, Silt, Clay)
  • ○ Sandy Soils: Have large pores, a high infiltration rate (water soaks in quickly)
  • and a low water-holding capacity (it drains out quickly). They require
  • frequent, small irrigation applications.
  • ○ Clay Soils: Have very fine pores, a low infiltration rate (water soaks in
  • slowly), and a high water-holding capacity (it stores water for longer). They
  • can handle less frequent, larger applications, but application rates must be
  • slow to prevent runoff.
  • ● Soil Depth: Deeper soils can store more water, meaning they can sustain a crop for
  • longer periods between irrigations compared to shallow soils.
  • ● Topography (Slope): Fields with steep or uneven slopes are prone to runoff and
  • erosion under surface irrigation (like flood). Pressurized systems (sprinkler or drip)
  • are often preferred as they allow for more controlled application on sloped terrain.
  • Essay Questions

questions.question: Write an essay on advantages and disadvantages of Intercropping.
questions.solution_html:
• Ans: Intercropping is a method of growing more than one crop in the same piece of
  • land during the same crop season. This is an environmentally friendly pest control
  • crop protection, and yield enhancement approach.
  • Advantages of intercropping
  • • Better utilization of growth resources like nutrients, light, and moisture.
  • • Mitigate losses where the failure of any one of the component crops occurs.
  • • A farmer can get extra yield and, thereby, extra income from the unit area.
  • • Better utilization of space is available with the time dimensions.
  • • We can achieve better weed control by growing intercrops.
  • • Minimizes the chances of soil crust formation.
  • • Mitigate losses where the failure of any one of the component crops occurs.
  • • Intercrops will also enhance soil fertility.
  • • Controls soil erosion.
  • • To some extent, the pests and diseases of the main crop are controlled.
  • • Ecological stability.
  • • Cultivation practices for the major crop will also supplement companion crop
  • requirements.
  • • It provides shading and physical support to some crops.
  • • It provides daily needs for the farmers.
  • Disadvantages of intercropping
  • • Sometimes, intercrops work as alternate hosts for various pests and diseases.
  • • Differential maturity and sometimes harvesting may become a problem.
  • • It becomes difficult to control various pests and diseases.
  • • Intercropping is a labor-intensive practice.
  • • Allelopathic effect. (Plants produce biochemicals that influence the growth and
  • reproduction of others.)
  • • Possibility of problems in carrying out intercultural operations.
  • • Difficulty in mechanization for processes like crop cutting, spraying, and irrigation.
  • • There might be competition among the component crops.
questions.final_answer: • There might be competition among the component crops
